messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: QA Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Vignette:
Eleanor presents as a meticulously dressed 73-year-old woman, her composure a stark contrast to the profound distress that has recently fractured the careful order of her life. For nearly sixty years, the events of her childhood were a sealed room in the house of her mind; she knew the door was there, but she had never tried the lock. That changed two months ago, at her sister-in-law's funeral. Standing by the open grave, the finality of the moment seemed to pry the door open, and the past came rushing into the present. The trauma, inflicted by her father throughout her early years, had remained a silent, managed weight until that day. Now, it is a constant, active presence.

The memories do not arrive as a story. Instead, Eleanor describes them as a series of still images that flash into her mind without warning. Remembering what happened, she explains, is just like looking at photographs of it: the glint of his belt buckle, the floral pattern on the wallpaper in the hallway, her own small scuffed shoes on the linoleum floor. Sometimes, these images are accompanied by a profound numbness; she can see the photograph of her own terrified face and feel absolutely nothing, as if it happened to a stranger she is merely observing. When her husband, concerned by her sudden withdrawal, asks what is wrong, Eleanor finds that she knows what happened but is unable to find the words to describe it. The narrative is lost, leaving only the brutal snapshots and a chasm of silence.

This re-emergence of the past has reconfigured her perception of the world as a landscape of imminent threat. At her job as a Quality Assurance Engineer, a role she has excelled in for decades due to its demand for precision and control, she now feels perpetually on edge. Her work environment, once a sanctuary of logic, has become a minefield. A sudden movement by a colleague in her peripheral vision puts her immediately on guard, her body tensing as if bracing for a blow. Her body reacts to danger before she has even had time to think; a junior engineer approaching her desk too quickly caused her to flinch so violently she knocked over her coffee, a physical reaction that preceded any conscious thought of threat. She has become superalert, her focus splintered as she constantly scans the office, tracking the movements of others.

The triggers are specific and pervasive. Being alone with men, even trusted colleagues in a professional setting, has become unbearable. She has started insisting on email correspondence for issues that would have once been a quick conversation, and she will delay project meetings until a female colleague can join, a behaviour that is beginning to strain relationships with her team. Uncertainty, the very thing her job is meant to eliminate, now feels like a personal threat. When a project's requirements are ambiguous, she experiences a surge of panic that is disproportionate to the professional stakes. It mirrors the terrifying unpredictability of her father's moods, a feeling she has spent a lifetime trying to engineer out of her existence.

Underpinning this daily struggle are deeply held beliefs that have crystallized over the decades, now spoken aloud for the first time. She has come to believe that she can’t stop bad things from happening to her, that she is fundamentally helpless against the malice or carelessness of others. This conviction is twinned with a crushing, illogical guilt. "I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened," she stated, the words heavy with the impossible burden a small child places upon herself. The foundation of it all is a sense of profound betrayal by the person who was supposed to be her ultimate protector. This feeling, dormant for so long, now colours her interactions and expectations, making trust feel like a dangerous gamble. Eleanor sought therapy after she found herself unable to enter a conference room for a one-on-one meeting with her male manager, standing frozen in the hallway. She is afraid she is losing the life she so carefully built and hopes, more than anything, to find a way to lock that door to the past again, this time for good.
